beats.t: Fifty thousand yeast lineages share one tube. Whenever a cell gains a beneficial mutation, its descendants start to take over.
Most of these mutations never become common enough to detect. In 2019, Nguyen Ba, Cvijović, Rojas Echenique and colleagues found a way to follow them anyway.
Their idea was to keep writing new DNA barcodes into the genome while evolution runs. This film walks through how it is done, and what it showed.

scenes.title: Why one barcode is not enough

beats.t: In a large asexual population, many beneficial mutations arise at once. Their lineages compete and most of them lose. This is clonal interference.
Sequencing the genomes of the whole population detects a mutation only once it passes a few percent. Most competing lineages never get that far.
Giving every cell a DNA barcode, as in Levy et al. 2015, resolves lineages down to about one cell in ten thousand.
But a barcode is inherited by every descendant. Once a lineage expands, later mutations inside it share its barcode and stay hidden.
The fix is to add fresh barcodes at intervals, so every lineage keeps splitting into newly labelled sublineages.
Start with a clonal population and give every cell a random barcode. Each barcode now labels a small lineage.
Let the population evolve for 100 generations. A few lineages grow, and most shrink.
Then insert a second barcode right beside the first. Every lineage splits into sublineages, each with its own label.
Repeat every 100 generations. Each cell carries a growing string of barcodes, one per round.
The string reads like a family tree. This is a real one from the YPD population: a founding barcode, then eight more, added 100 generations apart.
First, exactly one barcode locus per cell. A cell with two copies would carry two histories. Bacteria are hard to hold at one copy, so the authors chose budding yeast.
Haploid yeast often double their own genome over a long experiment, so the populations are diploid from the start, with the barcode locus on just one chromosome.
Second, no tight bottlenecks. If only a few cells were barcoded, the survivors would be a small random sample, and chance would reshuffle the competition.

Third, insertions that go one way and can be repeated ten times in the same place. In diploids a cut is usually healed by copying the other chromosome, so instead the authors used the recombinase Cre.
Cre recombinase swaps DNA between two lox sites. Two sites of the same kind react; two of different kinds, called orthogonal, ignore each other.
The authors used three orthogonal sites: loxP, lox5171 and lox2272. A landing pad in the genome waits with one of them.
A plasmid brings a new barcode flanked by matching sites. Cre lines them up and recombines, dropping the barcode into the landing pad.
The same reaction swaps the drug-resistance marker, so only cells that integrated correctly survive the next selection.
Cre is reversible: it can cut a barcode back out as easily as it put it in. For re-barcoding, each site must fire once and then switch off.
Each lox site has two arms that Cre grips. A mutation in one arm barely matters; mutations in both arms together abolish the site.
So the design arranges each reaction to combine two single-arm mutations into a double-arm mutant. The old site is inactivated, while a fresh orthogonal site is added for the next round.
The authors screened arm mutations and found one, lox2, that stays fully active paired with a normal arm but dies when paired with itself, exactly the switch they needed.
Because each round rewrites the locus, odd and even rounds need mirror-image plasmids. The authors built two, swapping the KanMX and HygMX drug markers each time.
On the plasmid the marker is broken: its start codon is missing. Only correct integration joins it to a start codon in the genome, through an artificial intron that must splice out.
A random 16-base barcode is dropped into each plasmid by a Golden Gate reaction. The library is grown in a thin layer of soft agar, giving over a million distinct barcodes.
Transform the population with the barcode library, selecting on soft agar for more than 100,000 colonies per population.
Switch to galactose for about 10 generations. Galactose turns on Cre, which performs the recombination.
Select on the new drug marker, so only recombined cells remain. Then counter-select with 5-FOA to throw away the spent plasmid.
Return the cells to the evolution medium. About 50,000 new barcodes have been written in, with no bottleneck tighter than the daily transfer.
Two diploid populations were founded from the same ancestor, each labelled with about 50,000 barcodes.
One grew in rich medium, YPD. The other in rich medium with acetic acid, YPA, which acidifies the cell and pushes selection harder.
Each day the culture was diluted 1 to 1024: about ten generations, through a bottleneck of roughly half a million cells.
A sample was frozen every day. Every 100 generations the population was re-barcoded. Each 100-generation block is called an epoch.
YPD ran for nine usable epochs, YPA for ten: nine hundred and a thousand generations of evolution.
DNA is extracted from each frozen sample and the barcode locus is amplified. Unique molecular identifiers tag each starting molecule so it is counted once.
The locus soon grows longer than one sequencing read. But the four newest barcodes fit in a single paired-end read.
Because barcodes are diverse, each new barcode is uniquely tied to its ancestors. The older labels were already sequenced, so the full string can be reassembled.
Sequencing errors are cleaned up by merging near-identical reads, leaving on average about 360,000 lineage counts per timepoint.
Here is the result for the YPA population: every barcoded sublineage that reached one in a thousand, stacked by frequency, colour chosen at random.
Grey bands are the barcoding rounds. Across each one, lineages fan out into finer sublineages.
There is structure everywhere, at every scale. But which of these wiggles are real selection, and which are just noise? That is the next problem.
Each lineage is a branching process. Between timepoints its count changes from two causes: selection, and chance.
Chance has two sources: the random sampling at each daily transfer, and the random sampling during DNA prep and sequencing. Together the authors call it drift.
Take all lineages near 40 reads and watch where they land next. Drift alone predicts a spread. The data match it, with one noise parameter kappa per interval.
Below about ten counts, a lineage is lost in this noise. Only once it climbs above it can selection be read from its slope.
A lineage grows relative to the population as its fitness exceeds the mean. On a log scale, the slope of its frequency is that fitness difference.
Any trajectory explained by drift alone is discarded, at a 5% false-discovery rate. The rest are fit jointly for their fitnesses and the population mean.
Grouping sublineages by their shared older barcodes averages out drift, so even small lineages give a usable fitness.
A new mutation makes a sublineage fitter than its parent, and all of its descendants inherit that edge. So compare each lineage with the one it split from.
When a child is reliably fitter than its parent, a mutation established between those two barcodes, within one 100-generation epoch.
Each such event founds a clone. In YPD the authors called 72 clones; in YPA, 124, nested inside one another many layers deep.
Now colour each lineage by its clone and stack them. This is the YPD population, redrawn from the called mutations. Stars mark where each one established.
Early on, many clones appear on the ancestral background and compete. Some pick up further mutations; a few stack several, interfering within their own parent clone.
Almost all of this is invisible to whole-population genome sequencing. Barcoding resolves it lineage by lineage.
Plot the population by fitness instead of by lineage. At each timepoint it is a distribution: a spread of fitnesses around a mean.
New mutations widen the spread; selection trims the slow lineages. The distribution holds its shape and marches to the right.
This is the travelling wave of adaptation that theory predicted, here watched directly for the first time.
In the simplest theory, the eventual winner is always near the leading edge of the wave. The data break that rule.
In YPA a lineage that was well behind acquired two strong mutations and leapfrogged everything ahead of it, sweeping to near fixation.
To check this was real, the authors re-evolved twelve populations from just before the sweep, without barcoding. All twelve replayed the same takeover.
A lineage's starting fitness only weakly predicts its fate. What matters more is whether it gains further mutations.
A fitter, faster-growing lineage is a larger, safer target: a new mutation in it is less likely to be lost to drift.
So fit backgrounds collect both weak and strong mutations, while slow ones need a rare strong hit to survive. Success compounds: the rich get richer.
In parallel, the whole population was genome-sequenced each epoch to name the genes under selection. Far fewer mutations clear the few-percent limit.
In YPA the targets fit the stress: BNA3, ASG1 and ASC1 are known to help cells tolerate acetic acid.
These few named mutations and the thousands of barcoded lineages tell one story at two resolutions.
By rewriting the genome as evolution ran, the authors followed competing lineages far below the limit of genome sequencing.
Adaptation moves as a travelling wave, but a disorderly one: lineages leapfrog, fortunes reverse, and early success compounds.
None of this fits the older models cleanly. Seeing it at all took a barcode you could write again, and again, and again.
